ch21.anchor: head of the China League for the Protection of Civil Rights
ch21.note: The China League for the Protection of Civil Rights (Zhongguo Minquan Baozhang Tongmeng), founded in Shanghai in December 1932 by Song Qingling, Cai Yuanpei, Lu Xun, and Yang Quan, was China’s first modern civil-liberties body; it worked to free political prisoners and to expose torture and secret trials. It survived only months: after its secretary-general Yang Quan was assassinated in June 1933 (see the following chapter) it effectively dissolved. Corroborated.
Author’s note. The passage is from Yang Zhihua (writing under the alias Du Ning), “The Course and Lessons of the Traitor Gu Shunzhang’s Defection,” Party Literature (Dang de wenxian), 1991, no. 3.

ch21.anchor: Chen Geng would not so much as glance at them.
ch21.note: Author’s note. From the American journalist Edgar Snow’s Random Notes on Red China.

ch21.anchor: for all the world like a man seizing stolen goods.
ch21.note: Author’s note. The reporter’s account is from “The Example of Shanghai Justice,” China Forum, vol. 2, no. 4, 13 April 1933. The China Forum was an English-language leftist weekly published in Shanghai and edited by Harold Isaacs, the “Harold Isaacs” of the League delegation named below.

ch21.anchor: it was Chen Geng who saved your life
ch21.note: The reference is to the Second Eastern Expedition of 1925: at the battle of Huatan, when Chiang Kai-shek’s column was routed, Chen Geng—then a Whampoa cadet on Chiang’s staff—is said to have carried the spent Chiang out of danger. The episode is widely told in Chinese accounts; Chiang never publicly acknowledged it. Corroborated in Communist sources; uncorroborated from Chiang’s side.

ch21.anchor: the Jiangsu No. 1 Model Prison at Laohuqiao
ch21.note: A modern Nanjing penitentiary at Laohuqiao that under the Nationalists held large numbers of political prisoners, women among them.

The Chinese Renaissance Society (Zhonghua Fuxingshe), better known as the Blue Shirts (Lanyishe), was a secret paramilitary organization set up within the Kuomintang in April 1932, modeled on the European Fascist movements, with Chiang Kai-shek as its head and Whampoa graduates at its core. Its special-services arm ran surveillance and assassination; it would murder Yang Xingfo in 1933 (see the following chapter). Corroborated.

ch21.anchor: president of the Military Engineering Institute of the Chinese People's Liberation Army
ch21.note: Chen Geng (1903–1961) went on to command armies in the war against Japan, the civil war, and Korea; in 1953 he founded and headed the PLA Military Engineering Institute at Harbin (the “Ha Jun Gong”), and in 1955 was made a general (da jiang).

A fanshengyuan (“self-examination institute”) was a Nationalist facility distinct from a prison, to which arrested Communists were transferred and pressed to sign a statement of repentance formally renouncing the Party in exchange for release.

The “Noulens affair.” “Hilaire Noulens” and his wife were arrested in the Shanghai International Settlement on 15 June 1931. His true name was Jakob Rudnik, a Soviet (Ukrainian-born) agent of the Comintern’s clandestine liaison service, funneling money and communications to Communist parties across the Far East; his wife was Tatiana Moissenko. The author’s “Poles” is mistaken—the couple’s real identity and nationality were then unknown. An international defense committee whose members included Albert Einstein, Song Qingling, and Henri Barbusse took up their case. Contrary to the impression given here, they were not freed after the prison hunger strike: sentenced to death, then commuted to life, they were released only in 1937. Contradicted in part.

ch21.anchor: already fallen beneath the enemy's bayonets
ch21.note: Wang Genying (1907–1939), a Shanghai textile worker and labor organizer who joined the Party in 1925 and married Chen Geng in 1927, was killed by Japanese troops at Nangong, southern Hebei, on 8 March 1939, having turned back for the unit’s funds and documents. Corroborated.

ch22.note: Ding Ling (1904–1986), pen name of Jiang Bingzhi, was among the most celebrated writers of the Chinese left. Abducted by Kuomintang agents on 14 May 1933 and held in Nanjing for three years, she escaped in 1936, with Feng Xuefeng’s help, to the Communist base at Bao’an. Her conduct in captivity was later questioned within the Party; the 1984 Central Committee resolution reproduced at the end of this section fully cleared her. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: won the approval of Lu Xun, Qu Qiubai, Mao Dun, and others.
ch22.note: Author’s note. The biographical sketch is from the Xinhua News Agency, “Life of Comrade Ding Ling,” People’s Daily, 16 March 1986.

ch22.anchor: the noted left-wing writer and Communist Hu Yepin
ch22.note: Hu Yepin (1903–1931), poet and Ding Ling’s companion, was one of the “Five Martyrs of the Left League,” young Communist writers secretly shot by the Nationalists at Longhua, Shanghai, on 7 February 1931. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: seared me with pain every day.
ch22.note: Author’s note. Ding Ling’s account of her captivity is from her memoir Wangliang shijie (“World of Demons”), in the Collected Works of Ding Ling, vol. 8.

ch22.anchor: was killed before the door of the Academia Sinica
ch22.note: Yang Quan (1893–1933), courtesy name Xingfo, a U.S.-trained scholar (Cornell and Harvard) and secretary-general both of Academia Sinica and of the China League for the Protection of Civil Rights, was shot dead in Shanghai on 18 June 1933 by Blue Shirt gunmen acting on Chiang Kai-shek’s order. His murder effectively ended the League. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: Taken with her was the philosopher Pan Zinian
ch22.note: Author’s note. Pan Zinian (1893–1972), a philosopher and journalist from Yixing, Jiangsu, joined the Party in 1927 and edited progressive journals; abducted with Ding Ling on 14 May 1933, he was freed in 1937 and went on to found and lead the Party’s Xinhua Daily in Wuhan and Chongqing. He was persecuted in the Cultural Revolution and died in prison.

ch22.anchor: the writer Ying Xiuren, who was calling on Ding Ling
ch22.note: Author’s note. Ying Xiuren (1900–1933), a poet of the “Lakeside” group, from Cixi in Zhejiang, was a Party member from 1925 and a figure in the League of Left-Wing Writers; he was killed on 14 May 1933, falling from Ding Ling’s building as he fought the agents who had come to abduct her.

ch22.anchor: it was this bullet that killed Yang.
ch22.note: Author’s note. The report is from Shen Bao, 19 June 1933.
Author’s note. From Israel Epstein, Soong Ching Ling: A Great Woman of the Twentieth Century (People’s Publishing House, 1992).

ch22.anchor: named one of them 'Guo Decheng Road.'
ch22.note: SACO—the Sino-American Cooperative Organization (Zhong-Mei suo)—was a joint Nationalist and U.S. intelligence and training body based at Chongqing during the war against Japan, run on the Chinese side by Dai Li’s Juntong. Its grounds held a notorious prison for Communists and other detainees.
